problem: Existing EQA agents and benchmarks assume clean, accurate human questions, but real users pose questions with wrong presumptions (misremembered attributes, non-existent objects, misperceived or substituted objects) that lead agents to fabricate answers or explore uselessly.
motivation: In real-world deployments such as assisting Alzheimer's patients or non-expert users, erroneous presumptions in questions cause wrong answers and even safety risks. Explore-EQA accuracy drops markedly on noisy questions compared with clean ones, yet no systematic taxonomy, benchmark or metric exists for this.
key_idea: Define a taxonomy of human question noise (latent hallucination, memory, perception, semantic), build a 500-question LLM-generated NoisyEQA benchmark with detection/correction metrics, and improve agents with plug-in Self-Correction prompting (NAP / NACoT).
insight: Prompting VLM agents to explicitly check questions against visual evidence lifts LLM-match accuracy substantially (e.g. GPT4o-EQA latent hallucination 51.59 to 87.60, DR 46.2 to 79.0). Nonexistent-object noise is mostly a detection problem, while perception and semantic noise stay hard to correct even when detected (CR remains far below humans at 93.4), so correction needs finer-grained reasoning. Noise also lowers answer confidence, which hurts view selection.
method: Noise taxonomy: Latent Hallucination Noise (non-existent objects) vs Active Noise, which splits into Memory (position, color, shape, counting, material), Perception, and Semantic noise.

LLM/template question generation: Wh- and yes/no templates; nonexistent objects inserted for hallucination noise; attributes replaced with wrong ones for memory noise; Gaussian-noised images described by GPT-4 to produce misidentified objects for perception noise; BERT top-10 similar objects with human selection by category overlap or functional association for semantic noise; two volunteers validated the data.
Reliable view selection: agent first answers a yes/no confidence question per view, and the probability of the 'yes' token selects the most reliable view for answering.
Noise Aware Prompt (NAP): appends a cognition prompt that reminds the agent to carefully check the question against the visual content.
Noise Aware Chain of Thought (NACoT): step-by-step verification of object existence, attributes, then function/semantics, with an explicit explanation of any detected noise before answering.
Evaluation: an LLM (GPT-4) scores answers 1-5 (noise detection, correction, accuracy); LLM-match accuracy C=mean((s-1)/4), Detection Rate (score>=3) and Correction Rate (score>=4).

setting.backbone: Llama2-EQA and GPT-4o-EQA (Prismatic-style DINO+SigLIP vision encoder with Llama-2 or GPT-4o), prompting only
setting.observation: multi-view RGB images of a scene with a text question
setting.action_space: none (open-ended text answers; no navigation actions evaluated)

numbers_note: Own benchmark (500 questions). Table 1 and Table 2 give LLM-match accuracy per noise type (e.g. GPT4o-EQA+NACoT latent hallucination 87.60, position 39.96, color 45.91, shape 49.19, counting 62.07, material 63.00, perception 45.00, semantic 51.02; humans 91.67/98.50/97.27/95.16/97.41/99.00/85.71/93.87). No overall accuracy is given. Human DR/CR 97.6/93.4. No navigation benchmark results.
results: Base agents perform poorly on noisy questions (GPT-4o-EQA DR 46.2 and CR 17.4; Llama2-EQA DR 3.0 and CR 2.8). Self-Correction prompting greatly improves them (GPT-4o+NAP DR 79.0, CR 42.0), but they remain well below humans (DR 97.6, CR 93.4), especially on active noise.
limitations: Small benchmark (500 questions) with static images only; no actual embodied exploration or navigation is evaluated
Requires token probabilities, so closed models like Gemini and Claude were excluded; only two agents were tested; the LLM-based judge may be biased
Correction rate stays low for perception and semantic noise, which the method does not solve
